facts.claim: RFC 3629 (2003): in UTF-8, the US-ASCII characters (plain English letters, digits and punctuation) take one byte each.
Jacob Ziv and Abraham Lempel published the pointer method now called LZ77 in 1977, in IEEE Transactions on Information Theory.
David Huffman published his method for building minimum-redundancy codes in the Proceedings of the IRE in 1952.
Byte pair encoding, the way many tokenizers build their vocabulary, began as a data compression algorithm (Sennrich, Haddow and Birch, 2016).
RFC 1951 (1996): DEFLATE packs data with the LZ77 pointers and Huffman codes together, with repeats of 3 to 258 bytes reaching back up to 32K bytes.
RFC 1952 (1996): a gzip file is DEFLATE data with a 10-byte header and an 8-byte trailer (a check number and the original size).
RFC 7932 (2016): Brotli also packs data with LZ77 pointers and Huffman codes together.
The Compression Streams standard (updated 19 October 2026) lets a web page compress with brotli, deflate, deflate-raw and gzip.
RFC 1951 (1996): a simple counting argument shows no lossless method can shrink every possible file.
Claude Shannon’s 1948 “A Mathematical Theory of Communication” defined entropy, the average bits per symbol no code can beat.
The JPEG committee describes JPEG as a Huffman-coded, DCT-based lossy image format.
RFC 1951 (1996): at worst, DEFLATE grows a file by 5 bytes per 32K-byte block, about 0.015% on large files.
RFC 1951 (1996): DEFLATE usually shrinks English text 2.5 to 3 times, to between two fifths and a third of its size.
The JPEG standard, CCITT T.81 (1992), cuts a picture into 8 × 8 blocks, turns each into 64 numbers and rounds each by its own step from a table.
RFC 8878 (2021) defines Zstandard, another lossless method, and registers “zstd” as a coding web servers may send files in.
